html:
The Alans were an Iranian-speaking nomad people of the steppe north of the Caucasus and the Black Sea, usually counted as a branch of the Sarmatians. Roman writers mention them from the first century CE. The map shows them at times from 100 to 1100.

Some Alans moved far west. When the Huns broke the Gothic kingdoms on the steppe around 375, groups of Alans fled or joined in the migrations. In 406 they crossed the Rhine into Gaul with the Vandals and Suebi, then went on into Spain. After the Visigoths beat them in 418 they joined the Vandals, whose kings were later styled "kings of the Vandals and Alans", and crossed with them to North Africa in 429.

The Alans who stayed in the North Caucasus built a kingdom of their own, Alania, shown on the map as the Caucasian Alans. It became Christian in the early 900s under Byzantine influence and was long linked with the Khazars. The Mongols destroyed it in the late 1230s. Survivors withdrew into the mountains, and the Ossetians of today descend from them and still speak an Iranian language.
